subjective.topic: The World Before Islam and Early Life
subjective.question: Write a note on the condition of the world and the Arabs before Islam.
subjective.answer: Before Islam there were no demarcated boundaries, no nations, states or governments and no interstate relations; people lived in small tribes and moved wherever they found food and fodder. The Arabs were ignorant and offensive, fighting battles over petty matters; every tribe considered itself superior and followed its own traditions, with no common law or virtuous leadership - the tribal chief held absolute authority. They had no formal education except local poetry and storytelling. They had forgotten Allah and worshipped idols - 360 idols stood in the Kaaba - besides the sun, moon, water and fire. Women were disrespected and even sold as slaves, female children were buried alive, and the poor were looked down upon.

subjective.topic: The World Before Islam and Early Life
subjective.question: How will you teach 'the World before Islam' to students of grades 1-4 and 5-8?
subjective.answer: For junior grades (1-4), whose minds are childish, the topic should be taught through story-type narration, because young children love stories; the teacher should make clear that it is not merely a story but truth, and should keep a polite and friendly attitude so that children learn in a healthy environment. For senior grades (5-8) a somewhat more serious attitude is needed, though never a repulsive tone. In both cases the teacher must keep the age factor, mental capacity and diverse backgrounds of the students in view, and at the end take feedback by asking a few questions, to know how much the students have grasped and what needs improvement.

subjective.topic: The World Before Islam and Early Life
subjective.question: Describe the Hajar-e-Aswad dispute and how the Prophet (S.A.W) solved it.
subjective.answer: When the Prophet (S.A.W) was thirty-five years old, the Quraish rebuilt the Kaaba, whose building had deteriorated. When the time came to place the Hajar-e-Aswad (the Black Stone) in its position, every tribe demanded the honour for itself, and bloodshed seemed certain. An old wise man suggested that the first person to enter the Kaaba the next morning should decide the matter. The first to enter was the Prophet (S.A.W), and everyone happily shouted 'Al-Sadiq, Al-Amin' (the truthful, the trustworthy). He spread a sheet of cloth on the ground, placed the stone in its centre, and asked a representative of every tribe to hold the sheet and carry it to the place; he then placed the stone in position with his own hands. Thus every tribe shared the honour, bloodshed was avoided, and his leadership was accepted by all.

subjective.question: Describe the event of the first revelation (Wahi).
subjective.answer: The Holy Prophet (S.A.W) used to retire to the Cave of Hira, about three miles from Mecca, to worship Allah in solitude. At the age of forty, in the month of Ramadan, the angel Hazrat Jibril (A.S) appeared before him and commanded him to read. The Prophet (S.A.W) replied that he could not read. The angel embraced him tightly, chest to chest, three times, repeating the command, and then recited the first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq, which the Prophet (S.A.W) repeated after him until he had learnt them by heart. This was the beginning of the revelation of the Holy Quran and of his mission as the Messenger of Allah. Hazrat Jibril (A.S) also taught him Wudu and Salat before departing.

subjective.question: With whom did the Prophet (S.A.W) first share the experience of the first Wahi, and how was he comforted?
subjective.answer: On returning home, the Prophet (S.A.W) was shivering with fear and asked to be covered with a blanket. He narrated the whole incident to his wife Hazrat Khadija (R.A), who comforted him, saying that he had never done wrong to anyone, was kind to others and helped the poor, so Allah would never let him down. The next morning she took him to her cousin Warqa bin Nofal, a learned Christian who had studied the Bible. Warqa confirmed that the visitor was the same angel who had come to Hazrat Musa (A.S) and other prophets, and that Allah had chosen Muhammad (S.A.W) as His Prophet; he also warned that his people would oppose him and expel him.

subjective.question: What was the first speech of the Prophet (S.A.W) before the Quraish on Koh-e-Safa?
subjective.answer: Standing on the hill of Safa near the Kaaba, the Prophet (S.A.W) asked the people of Mecca what they thought of him. They replied that he was Al-Sadiq and Al-Amin (the truthful and the trustworthy). He then asked whether they would believe him if he told them an army was behind the hill ready to attack them; they said yes. Thereupon he invited them to believe in Allah, to say 'La ilaha illa Allah', to give up idols and evil practices and to do good deeds, warning them of the Day of Judgement. Abu Lahab reacted angrily, saying that he had wasted their time, and the Quraish became his enemies.

subjective.question: What do you know about Hazrat Zaid bin Haris (R.A)?
subjective.answer: Hazrat Zaid (R.A) was a slave whom Hazrat Khadija (R.A) gave to the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) at the time of her marriage. The Prophet (S.A.W) immediately set him free, but when his father and relatives came to take him back, he refused to leave, saying he had seen such qualities in the Prophet (S.A.W) that he would never choose anyone over him. He was the first among the slaves to embrace Islam. He remained in the close company of the Prophet (S.A.W), and later the Prophet (S.A.W) appointed him commander of the Muslim army in the Battle of Mu'tah, where he embraced martyrdom.

subjective.question: Describe the stay of the Prophet (S.A.W) in the Cave of Saur during the Hijrat.
subjective.answer: Knowing that the Quraish would search for them in the morning, the Prophet (S.A.W) and Hazrat Abu Bakr (R.A) hid in the Cave of Saur near Mecca and stayed there for three days. By the command of Allah, a spider wove its web at the mouth of the cave, a Babul tree grew up covering the entrance, and two pigeons built a nest on the tree and laid eggs, so that the search parties concluded the place had been lying vacant and barren for a long time and passed by. Hazrat Asma (R.A), the elder sister of Hazrat Ayesha (R.A), brought them food, while Abdullah, the son of Hazrat Abu Bakr (R.A), spent the nights in the cave and returned to the city each morning to gather news of the Quraish's activities, reporting back at night. On the fourth day they resumed the journey to Madina with the guide Abdullah bin Areqat.

subjective.question: Describe the incident of Suraqa bin Malik during the Hijrat.
subjective.answer: The Quraish had announced a reward of 100 camels for anyone who arrested the Prophet (S.A.W) and brought him to them. Suraqa bin Malik spotted the Prophet (S.A.W) after he left the Cave of Saur and rode after him to arrest him, but the feet of his horse bogged down in the ground; this happened again and again, and the third time Suraqa himself fell down. The Prophet (S.A.W) then said to him: 'What do you think, O Suraqa, of the day when you will wear the precious bangles of Khusro, the emperor of Iran?' Suraqa begged forgiveness, which the Prophet (S.A.W) granted at once, and he embraced Islam. Fourteen years later, in the caliphate of Hazrat Umar (R.A), the prophecy was fulfilled and the bangles of Khusro were given to Suraqa.

subjective.question: What was the response of the Ansar when the Prophet (S.A.W) reached Madina?
subjective.answer: When the Prophet (S.A.W) reached Quba, the Ansar families gathered around him shouting 'Allah-o-Akbar' and paid him emotionally respectful regards; many Sahaba stayed there as guests of the family of Amr bin Auf. On entering Madina, all the Ansar came out to welcome the Messenger of Allah, and every tribe wished that he would stay at their house. It finally fell to the luck of Hazrat Abu Ayub Ansari (R.A), at whose house the Prophet (S.A.W) stayed for seven months. The Ansar's hospitality was unexampled: they competed with one another in serving him; the mother of Hazrat Anas (R.A) presented her whole property to him, which he accepted and immediately donated to his nurse Umm-e-Aiman (R.A). The Ansar also made the Muhajireen their brothers through Muakhaat and behaved with them like blood relations.

subjective.question: What were the salient features of the Treaty of Madina (Mesaaq-e-Madina)?
subjective.answer: The Prophet (S.A.W) made this treaty between the Muslims (Ansar) and the Jews of Madina (Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir and Banu Quraiza) so that all could live peacefully and future dangers could be neutralised. Its salient features were: (1) atonement and ransom would remain unchanged; (2) the Jews would have complete religious independence and nobody would interfere in their religion; (3) Jews and Muslims would remain friendly with each other; (4) if a third force attacked either party, both would help each other; (5) no party would provide shelter to the Quraish; (6) if anyone attacked Madina, both parties would join in its defence; and (7) if one party forgave an enemy, the other would also forgive, except in a religious battle.

subjective.question: Write a note on the expulsion of the Jewish tribes from Madina.
subjective.answer: The Jewish tribes of Madina had signed the Treaty of Madina with the Muslims, but they constantly violated it. When their sympathies and secret support for the Quraish of Mecca were established, two tribes - Banu Qaynuqa and Banu Nadir - were expelled from Madina, and the treaty no longer remained effective for them. After their expulsion they settled by design in the border areas of Khyber and Syria, from where they could observe movements to and from Madina and inform the Quraish. They also instigated the Quraish to attack Madina and promised them complete help, which led to Ghazwa-e-Ahzab; during that battle the remaining tribe, Banu Quraiza, also broke the treaty and sided with the enemy.

subjective.question: Compare the armies of the Muslims and the non-believers in the Battle of Badr.
subjective.answer: The Battle of Badr (17th Ramadan, 2 A.H) was the first formal battle between the Muslims and the Kuffar. The Muslim army was small and ill-equipped: 313 men, only 6 swords, 70 camels and 2 horses; 82 of them were Muhajireen and the rest Ansar, and they had no intention of fighting a war. The Kuffar, by contrast, were well equipped: 1000 men, 100 horses, 600 jackets (armour) and hundreds of camels. In spite of this great difference, the Muslims won: 70 Kuffar were killed and 70 taken prisoner, while only 14 Muslims were martyred.

subjective.question: Describe the performance of the Muslims in the Battle of Badr.
subjective.answer: The Muslims displayed unexampled bravery at Badr. First Hazrat Ali (R.A), Hazrat Hamza (R.A) and Hazrat Ubaida bin Haris (R.A) fought single combats against Utbah, Sheeba and Waleed bin Utbah and killed them; then the general battle began. Two young Muslims, Maaz and Muawwaz, killed Abu Jahal, the commander of the Kuffar army. Angels also helped the Muslims. The Prophet (S.A.W) treated the prisoners wonderfully: some were freed as a courtesy, others were released on fidya (ransom), and those who could not pay were told to teach reading and writing to ten Muslim children each and go free. Thus 313 poorly equipped men defeated a fully equipped army of 1000, proving that Allah never leaves His believers alone.

subjective.question: What happened in the Battle of Uhud? Explain briefly.
subjective.answer: The Battle of Uhud was fought on 7th Shawwal, 3 A.H at Mount Uhud, about 5 km north of Madina, by the Quraish to avenge Badr. The Prophet (S.A.W) set out with 1000 men, but Abdullah bin Ubai, the leader of the hypocrites, deserted with 300, leaving 700 Muslims against 3000 Kuffar, 3000 camels and 200 horses under Abu Sufyan. The Prophet (S.A.W) posted 50 archers on a mountain pass with strict orders not to leave it in victory or defeat. The Muslims initially prevailed, but most archers left the pass to collect booty; only 10 remained, and Khalid bin Waleed attacked through the pass from behind. Hazrat Hamza (R.A) was martyred by the slave Wahshi. A rumour of the Prophet's (S.A.W) martyrdom spread but was soon disproved; the Muslims regrouped and the Kuffar withdrew.

subjective.question: What was the performance of the Muslim women in the Battle of Uhud?
subjective.answer: The Muslim ladies played a great role in the Battle of Uhud. Hazrat Ayesha (R.A) and Hazrat Umm-e-Saleem (R.A), the mother of Hazrat Anas (R.A), devoted themselves to providing water to the wounded - never an easy task in a battlefield. Umm-e-Saleet, the mother of Hazrat Abu Saeed Khudri (R.A), performed the same duty. When only a few soldiers were left around the Prophet (S.A.W), Hazrat Umm-e-Ammara (R.A) reached him and stood in front of him to protect him, stopping the attacking Kuffar with her sword and arrows; she was seriously injured in this by Ibn-e-Qammaya. Their services show that the women of the early Muslim community shared fully in its sacrifices.

subjective.question: How will you teach the Battle of Badr to students of grades 1-4?
subjective.answer: Junior students are not well aware of countries, their frontiers and the names of opponents, so the teacher should begin by showing them the countries and making them remember the names of the famous countries and the opposing sides. They should also be taught the names of the commanders, their character and the instructions of the Prophet (S.A.W), because this builds a knowledge base which will make the senior-class lessons easy to understand. Narration should remain simple and story-like, and the juniors should be given the task of remembering Surah-e-Kausar by heart.

subjective.question: How will you teach the battles to students of grades 5-8?
subjective.answer: Senior students probably know many basic things, but there is no harm in quickly repeating them. Students of grades 5-8 should be told to remember the war itself, the enemies, the causes of the war, its results and its aftermath. They should be made to memorise Surah Al-Kafirun, given proper time for it, and the teacher should listen to them and ensure that their pronunciation is correct. Along with reading and writing, understanding is important for these students, and they should keep adding correctly pronounced memorised portions of the Holy Quran with the passage of time.

subjective.question: How will you teach the Battle of Mu'tah to students of grades 5-8?
subjective.answer: Following the method prescribed for teaching battles to senior grades, the teacher should first revise the background - the Prophet's (S.A.W) letters to the rulers and the martyrdom of his envoy Hazrat Haris bin Umair (R.A) at the hands of Shurjeel bin Amr. Students should be made to remember the essentials: the date (Jamadi-ul-Awal, 8 A.H), the place (Mu'tah in Syria, famous for its swords), the strength of the two armies (3,000 Muslims against about 100,000), the appointed commanders in order - Hazrat Zaid bin Haris (R.A), Hazrat Jafar-e-Tayyar (R.A) and Hazrat Abdullah bin Rawaha (R.A) - and the bravery of Hazrat Khalid bin Waleed (R.A), who broke eight swords, earned the title Saifullah and withdrew the army safely. Causes, results and aftermath should be discussed, and the students' memorisation should be heard and corrected.

subjective.question: What do you know about the valley of Hunain? Describe Ghazwa-e-Hunain briefly.
subjective.answer: Hunain is a valley about 40 kilometres from Mecca. After Fateh Mecca, the two powerful tribes of the area, Hawazin and Thaqif, instead of embracing Islam, prepared to attack Mecca; their leader Malik bin Auf camped with all his belongings at the valley of Autas near Hunain. The Prophet (S.A.W) marched on 6th Shawwal, 8 A.H with 12,000 men (10,000 who had come for Fateh Mecca and 2,000 new Muslims). Reaching the valley at night, the Muslims were surprised by a rain of arrows from the enemy hidden in scattered positions and began to scatter. The Prophet (S.A.W) stood firm, saying 'It is not a lie, I am a Prophet, I am the son of Abdul Muttalib', and Hazrat Abbas (R.A) called the people of Bai'at-e-Rizwan back; the Muslims reconsolidated, the Prophet (S.A.W) threw dust towards the enemy, and the enemy was defeated - 70 men of Banu Thaqif were killed and their families and goods became booty.

subjective.question: Write a note on the steadfastness and firmness of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) at Hunain.
subjective.answer: At Hunain the Muslim army, surprised by the enemy's arrows in the darkness, scattered very badly, and it seemed impossible to gather it again; only about ten men remained around the Prophet (S.A.W). In this hue and cry the Prophet (S.A.W) demonstrated complete firmness and confidence: instead of retreating, he kept moving ahead towards the Kuffar, declaring, 'It is not a lie, I am a Prophet (S.A.W), I am the son of Abdul Muttalib.' His steadfastness became the centre around which the army rallied when Hazrat Abbas (R.A) called the Sahaba back, and the battle ended in victory. The lesson of Hunain is that one should never become proud of one's strength and never forget Allah.

subjective.question: How did the Muslims win the Battle of Tabuk?
subjective.answer: In 9 A.H the Roman emperor Herqul prepared an army of 40,000 to crush the Muslims. Despite a year of famine, the Muslims prepared for jihad with unexampled donations: Hazrat Abu Bakr (R.A) gave everything he had, Hazrat Umar (R.A) half of his property, and Hazrat Usman (R.A) 900 camels, 100 horses, 1000 dinars and 200 ouqia of silver. An army of 30,000 marched the 500 miles to Tabuk, 18 men sharing a single camel. When the Romans learnt of these solid preparations, they were demoralised and, after deliberation, withdrew without fighting rather than face certain defeat and disgrace. The Prophet (S.A.W) stayed at Tabuk for 20 days and returned to Madina; thus the Muslims won the battle without fighting it.

subjective.question: How will you teach Ghazwa-e-Tabuk to students of grades 5-8?
subjective.answer: The teacher should explain the causes (the Roman preparations under Herqul), the difficult circumstances (the year of famine) and the spirit of sacrifice shown in the donations of the Sahaba, then the march of 30,000 Muslims over 500 miles with 18 men sharing one camel, and finally the result - the Romans withdrew and the Muslims won without a battle, staying at Tabuk for 20 days. Students should be made to remember the war, its enemies, causes, results and aftermath, memorise Surah Al-Kafirun with correct pronunciation, and the lesson that sincere preparation and trust in Allah bring success should be emphasised.

subjective.question: How will you teach Ghazwa-e-Ahzab and the trench to students of grades 5-8?
subjective.answer: The teacher should first explain why the confederates (Ahzab) attacked: revenge for Badr and Uhud and the threat to the Quraish trade routes to Syria and Iraq. Then describe the geography of Madina - protected on three sides, open only from the north - and Hazrat Salman Farsi's (R.A) suggestion of digging a trench on the open side, in whose digging the Prophet (S.A.W) himself took part. The main events should be narrated: the 10,000-strong confederate army camped before the trench; Amr bin Abd-e-Wadd crossed it and was killed by Hazrat Ali (R.A); Banu Quraiza broke the treaty; Hazrat Safia (R.A) killed a Jew who came to attack the women and children; and the confederates finally withdrew, with only six Muslim martyrs. Students should retain the causes, course, results and aftermath of the battle.

subjective.question: What is the meaning of Bai'at-e-Rizwan? Describe the incident.
subjective.answer: When the Prophet (S.A.W) camped at Hudaybiyyah with 1400 Muslims to perform Umrah, he sent Hazrat Usman (R.A) to the Quraish to explain that they had come for Umrah, not war. Hazrat Usman (R.A) stayed three days, and a rumour spread that he had been martyred. The Muslims were deeply grieved and emotional, and the Prophet (S.A.W), sitting under a tree, took a pledge (bai'at) from the Sahaba that they would take revenge for Hazrat Usman (R.A). This pledge is called Bai'at-e-Rizwan, and it is mentioned in Surah Al-Fath: 'Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree.'

subjective.question: What is Fateh-e-Mubeen? How did it occur?
subjective.answer: Fateh-e-Mubeen ('a clear, manifest victory') is the name the Holy Quran gives to the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah in verse 1 of Surah Al-Fath. Although the terms of the treaty appeared to favour the Quraish, it ended the state of war and opened interaction between the two sides: separated families began visiting Madina and Mecca for months, and the Meccans, impressed by the Muslims' behaviour, hospitality and clean character, embraced Islam in numbers never seen before - among them Hazrat Khalid bin Waleed (R.A) and Hazrat Amr bin Aas (R.A). The ten-year peace thus spread Islam more than war had done, which is why Allah called the treaty a clear victory.

subjective.question: Write down the main conditions of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.
subjective.answer: (1) The Muslims would return to Madina that year without performing Umrah. (2) They would come the next year, stay only three days in Mecca and perform Umrah. (3) They would bring no displayed weapons; swords would remain in sheaths, tied in bags. (4) No Muslim from Mecca would be taken to Madina, and a person going from Madina to Mecca would not be returned, while anyone coming to Madina from Mecca would be returned. (5) All Arab tribes were free to join either party. (6) There would be no war between the Muslims and the Quraish for ten years. The treaty was written by Hazrat Ali (R.A) for the Muslims and negotiated by Suhail bin Amr for the Quraish.

subjective.question: What does the Holy Quran say about the women in connection with the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah?
subjective.answer: The treaty had made no mention of women, although women could also migrate. The Holy Quran guided the Muslims in Surah Al-Mumtahina (verse 10): when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them; if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers, for they are not lawful for the disbelievers nor are the disbelievers lawful for them; but give the disbelievers what they spent (the dower). There is no blame upon you if you marry them when you have given them their due compensation, and do not hold to marriage bonds with disbelieving women. This is the judgement of Allah, who is Knowing and Wise.

subjective.topic: Fateh Mecca and the Last Sermon
subjective.question: Describe the events of Fateh Mecca (the Conquest of Mecca).
subjective.answer: When Banu Bakr, allies of the Quraish, attacked Banu Khuza'a, the allies of the Muslims, the Prophet (S.A.W) offered the Quraish three options: pay blood money (khoon-baha) to Banu Khuza'a, withdraw support from Banu Bakr, or set aside the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The Quraish hastily chose the third, then regretted it and sent Abu Sufyan to Madina to renew the treaty, but he failed. On 10th Ramadan, 8 A.H, the Prophet (S.A.W) marched with 10,000 men and camped at Marr-uz-Zuhran, where fires were lit over a wide area. Abu Sufyan was arrested, brought to the Prophet (S.A.W) and embraced Islam. The Prophet (S.A.W) announced safety for whoever took shelter in Abu Sufyan's house, closed his door, entered Masjid-e-Haram or surrendered. Entering Mecca, he took the key of the Kaaba from Usman bin Talha, kissed the Hajar-e-Aswad, performed Tawaf and broke the 360 idols reciting 'Truth has arrived and falsehood has vanished', then addressed the Quraish in Khutba-e-Fateh, declaring a general amnesty: 'Today there is no blame on you; go, you are all free.'

subjective.topic: Fateh Mecca and the Last Sermon
subjective.question: How will you teach the Conquest of Mecca to students of grades 1-4?
subjective.answer: For junior students the teacher should first show the location of Mecca and the Khana Kaaba with the help of a good teaching aid or map, since a common student may never have seen one. The events should be narrated simply, stressing that prayer is due to Allah alone and not to idols, that idols are only statues of clay and stone which can neither give nor take anything, and that the Holy Prophet (S.A.W) is the last Messenger of Allah. Special stress should be laid on the Prophet's (S.A.W) kindness: the Quraish were his worst enemies, yet he forgave them all and harmed no one. Students should be asked to write the difficult words in their notebooks, and their work should be checked.

subjective.topic: Fateh Mecca and the Last Sermon
subjective.question: How will you teach the Conquest of Mecca to students of grades 5-8?
subjective.answer: For senior students the teacher should explain the background - the violation of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah by Banu Bakr's attack on Banu Khuza'a and the three options offered to the Quraish - followed by the march of 10,000 Muslims, the camp at Marr-uz-Zuhran, Abu Sufyan's acceptance of Islam, the safety announcement, the cleansing of the Kaaba from the 360 idols and the general amnesty of Khutba-e-Fateh. Locations should be shown on a map or globe so that students grasp distances and places. The moral lessons - forgiveness at the height of power, mercy instead of revenge, and prayer to Allah alone - should be drawn out in discussion, and students should be made to remember the causes, events, results and aftermath of the conquest.

subjective.topic: Fateh Mecca and the Last Sermon
subjective.question: What are the main points of the Last Sermon (Khutba Hajjatul Wida)?
subjective.answer: The Last Sermon was delivered at Arafat on 9th Zil-Hajj, 10 A.H, during the Prophet's (S.A.W) only Hajj. Its main points are: the life and property of every Muslim are a sacred trust, like this day, month and city; goods entrusted to you must be returned to their rightful owners; hurt no one so that no one hurts you; always remember the Hereafter, for you will meet Allah and He will reckon your deeds; interest (riba) is forbidden and all interest obligations are waived; beware of Satan in small things; treat women well and kindly, for husbands and wives have rights over each other; worship Allah, offer the five daily prayers, fast in Ramadan, give Zakat and perform Hajj if you are able; no Arab has superiority over a non-Arab and no white over a black except by piety and good action, and every Muslim is a brother to every Muslim; no prophet will come after him; and he left behind two things - the Quran and his Sunnah - following which the Muslims will never go astray. He ended by asking the people to pass his words on to others and called Allah to witness that he had conveyed the message.
